newsitem.title: USA: Rubin downplays economic risks of stock market rise.
newsitem.headline: Rubin downplays economic risks of stock market rise.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin Monday played down worries that the steep run-up in the stock market posed risks for the economy and foresaw continued good economic times ahead.
In a wide-ranging interview with Reuters, Rubin also reitreated his support for a strong dollar and stressed the importance of balancing the federal government budget.

"It's always hard to judge what an economy is going to do," Rubin said, adding, "It looks to me like conditions are good and the most likely scenario is that they will continue to be good so long as we continue with sensible things."

The rosy outlook for the economy has helped propel Wall Street stock prices ever higher in recent weeks, shattering record after record. The Dow Jones industrial average of leading shares rose 76.03 points on Monday to a record 6,547.79.

The steep run-up -- blue-chip stock prices have soared more than 25 percent this year -- has led some economists to worry that the market is setting itself up for a crash that could cripple the economy.

While declining to say whether he thought stock prices have risen too far, the former Wall Street executive argued that what was important were the economic fundamentals, not the level of the market per se.
"I don't have any great crystal ball," Rubin said. "Markets over time reflect fundamentals. What we need to do is focus on the fundamentals."
That means following what Rubin called sensible policies, including balancing the budget, respecting the independence of the Federal Reserve and supporting a strong dollar.

American manufacturing companies sharply criticised the strong-dollar policy last week, arguing that the currency's steep 40 percent rise against the Japanese yen over the past 1-1/2 years was damaging U.S. exports and economic growth.
Rubin said, however, that the administration had no plans to change or de-emphasise its support for a strong dollar in Clinton's second four-year term.
"A strong dollar helps to keep interest rates down, helps to keep inflation down," he said. "It's very much in our interest."

A strong dollar holds down the price of imports. It also helps reassure foreign investors that they will not lose money from currency swings if they put cash in U.S. bonds. And that holds down American interest rates.
The Treasury chief said it was too soon to say whether the administration and the Republican-led Congress would be able to strike a deal to balance the budget.
"It's too early to know how all this is going to work out," he said.
The budget deficit unexpectedly shrank to $107 billion in the 1996 fiscal year that just ended on Sept. 30, thanks in part to a surge in individual income tax receipts.
Speaking to reporters last week, White House Budget Director Frank Raines was upbeat that tax receipts would remain strong.
Rubin though seemed more cautious and said that the Treasury expected to have additional information on hand next month to better assess the outlook for government revenues.
